hero.subtitle: A forest temple north of Krabi town where 1,237–1,260 steps (counts vary by source) lead to a golden Buddha and an open viewpoint over the Andaman Sea.

intro.title: About Wat Tham Suea — Krabi's Most Famous Forest Temple
intro.welcome: Welcome to Wat Tham Suea, widely recognized as the central Krabi Wat Tham Suea. Located in the heart of Krabi, Krabi Province, Thailand, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the region.
intro.description: Wat Tham Suea sits among the limestone hills about 7 km north of Krabi town. It is both a busy southern-Thai Buddhist temple and a popular hiking destination, blending dramatic natural caves, a golden Buddha and a serene meditation atmosphere.

highlights.title: Why Visit
items: Climb 1,237 steps to the summit with views over the Krabi plain and the Andaman Sea
A 9-metre golden Buddha and the legendary tiger footprints at the top
Still an active forest monastery with natural caves and shrines
Limestone caverns, stalactites and a peaceful, retreat-like atmosphere

guide.title: Before You Go
guide.description: The temple is visitor-friendly, but as a religious site there are a few things worth knowing in advance.
items: Cover shoulders and knees; remove shoes inside the main hall
The climb takes 30–60 minutes on steep, unshaded steps — go early or late
Wild macaques live along the route; do not feed or provoke them
Carry enough water; the steps can be slippery in places

visit.title: Hours, Accessibility & How to Visit Wat Tham Suea in Krabi
visit.subtitle: The temple is open all year with no booking needed. To ensure all visitors have a comfortable experience, we provide detailed layout and accessibility information.
visit.addressValue: 35 Krabi Noi, Mueang Krabi District, Krabi 81000 Thailand
visit.accessibilityText: While the summit requires a strenuous climb of 1,237 steps, the main hall at the base, parts of the natural caves, and the centuries-old bodhi tree paths in the valley monastery are flat and highly suitable for elderly visitors, wheelchair users, or those with limited stamina.
visit.mapLayoutText: The grounds are clearly laid out: spacious parking and restrooms are near the entrance; heading left leads to the natural caves and flat forest meditation paths; heading right takes you to the starting point of the 1,237-step climb.

transport.title: How to Reach Wat Tham Suea
transport.subtitle: The temple is about 7 km from Krabi town and easy to reach by car, taxi or local songthaew.
transport.overview: Whether you stay in Krabi town, Ao Nang or Railay, getting to Tiger Cave Temple is straightforward. Here are the three most common and hassle-free options.

modes.title: Songthaew / Taxi
modes.description: The most common local ride — flexible and cheap.
details: Blue songthaews in town run shared trips, about 40–60 THB one way
A private taxi round trip is around 300–500 THB and waits for you
Most hotels can call a taxi or arrange a private car

modes.title: Motorbike Rental
modes.description: The most free way, with scenic roads along the way.
details: Motorbikes rent for about 200–300 THB per day in town
Head north on Route 4034 for about 7 km; signage is clear
Free parking on site; watch the winding hill road

modes.title: Tour / Day Trip
modes.description: Ideal if you want it arranged and combined with other stops.
details: Island-hopping, rock-climbing and elephant camps often add a stop here
A half-day private tour can pair the temple with hot springs nearby
Confirm with the operator that Tiger Cave Temple is included

tips.title: Practical advice for a smoother visit
tips.subtitle: Wat Tham Suea is open to visitors yet remains an active place of worship. Following this code of conduct helps you climb safely while respecting local ecology and beliefs.

cards.title: Dress & Etiquette
cards.text: Cover shoulders and knees on temple grounds and remove shoes inside the main hall; keep strict silence and show respect near meditation areas and monks.

cards.title: Summit Prep
cards.text: The 1,237 steps are steep and mostly unshaded — wear trainers and bring water. The climb takes 30–60 min; rest in the shade when needed.

cards.title: Strictly No Feeding Macaques
cards.text: To protect the natural foraging habits and health of wild macaques, feeding is strictly prohibited. Keep glasses, phones, and small items secure to prevent snatching.

cards.title: Leave No Trace
cards.text: Practice 'Leave No Trace' principles. Do not leave any trash on the hill; bring all waste back down to the base to protect the pristine forest ecology.

support.title: Supporting Daily Operations
support.subtitle: The maintenance, ecological conservation, and support for monks at Wat Tham Suea rely entirely on public donations. Your kindness directly helps sustain this place of faith and nature.

items.title: Steps & Facilities Maintenance
items.description: The 1,237 steps to the summit and the viewpoint face constant weather erosion and require ongoing maintenance to ensure safety for all climbers.

items.title: Ecological & Forest Protection
items.description: As part of a nature reserve, the temple helps clear forest litter, protects wildlife habitats, and maintains a pure 'Leave No Trace' ecology.

items.title: Monastic Life & Temple Operations
items.description: Supports the daily meals, medical care, and meditation needs of resident monks, as well as basic operations like nighttime lighting and utilities.

support.donationText: Wat Tham Suea does not charge an entrance fee. If you wish to support, donation boxes are located at the main hall entrance, near the natural caves, and beside the summit Buddha. All funds go directly to temple maintenance and public welfare.

events.title: A Living Forest Monastery
events.subtitle: Wat Tham Suea is not just a scenic spot but a vital religious center. Grand ceremonies are held here during major Buddhist festivals.

festivals.name: Makha Bucha
festivals.desc: Commemorates the Buddha's teaching to 1,250 enlightened monks. Devotees hold candlelit processions around the stupas and caves at the base.

festivals.name: Visakha Bucha
festivals.desc: The most sacred festival celebrating the birth, enlightenment, and nirvana of the Buddha. Many devotees hike to the summit Buddha on this day.

festivals.name: Vipassana Meditation
festivals.desc: Continuing the Forest Tradition, the temple offers meditation guidance. The valley monastery sometimes hosts devotees for short-term retreats.

bestTime.title: When is it most comfortable?
bestTime.subtitle: Timing your visit avoids the heat and catches the best light and sunsets. Here's how to plan by time of day and by season.

day.label: Early morning 06:00–09:00
day.text: Arrive at opening for cool, uncrowded steps and soft light — the most pleasant window to climb and photograph.

day.label: Midday 11:00–15:00
day.text: The stairs are almost fully exposed and the heat is intense; the summit climb is tough, so try to avoid it.

day.label: Late afternoon 16:00–18:00
day.text: Climb for sunset as golden light spills across the Krabi plain — the most memorable moment of the day.

season.label: Cool season (Nov–Feb)
season.text: Dry and comfortable — ideal for the climb, but also peak tourist season, so arrive early.

season.label: Hot season (Mar–May)
season.text: High temperatures and strong UV — go at dawn or dusk and carry plenty of water.

season.label: Rainy season (May–Oct)
season.text: Green and quiet with fewer crowds, but steps get slippery — wear grippy shoes and take care.

history.title: History & Significance of Wat Tham Suea
history.subtitle: From a meditating monk's retreat to a bustling hillside monastery, the story of Wat Tham Suea is as intriguing as its name — part documented history, part legend passed down for decades.

sections.title: Birth of a Forest Monastery (1975)
sections.content: In 1975, the renowned southern-Thai meditation monk Luang Pho Jamnian Silasettho (หลวงพ่อจำเนียร ศิลาเสถโร) settled in a natural cave amid the limestone hills north of Krabi Town. Following the Thai Forest Tradition of simplicity, meditation and living close to nature, he gradually drew devotees from far and wide, and the once-remote grotto grew into the forest monastery seen today. Luang Pho Jamnian passed away in Malaysia on 18 August 2026 at the age of 90, according to Thai media reports.

sections.title: How It Got Its Name
sections.content: Legend says that when the monk first arrived, tigers still roamed the caves; clawed markings scarred the rock walls, and one stalactite is shaped uncannily like a crouching tiger. The temple was thus named Wat Tham Suea — literally 'Tiger Cave Temple' in Thai — a name that both records Krabi's wild forested past and lends the site an air of mystery.

sections.title: 1,237 Steps & the Summit Buddha
sections.content: The temple's most famous feature is the steep 1,237-step staircase up Khao Kaeo hill. At the top, a roughly 9-metre seated golden Buddha (Phra Puttakhaya Sirirat) presides over the clouds, surrounded by gilded images, a Buddha footprint and a giant carved footprint. From about 278 m, the summit offers a 360° panorama of the Krabi plain, winding rivers and the distant karst peaks of the Andaman Sea.

sections.title: Caves, Bodhi Trees & Ancient Giants
sections.content: Beyond the summit Buddha, the base of the hill is ringed by a network of natural caverns (tham means 'cave'), enshrining Buddha images, relics and monks' belongings. A forested loop trail leads to a serene 'valley monastery', shaded by bodhi and towering yang trees said to be centuries old — a cool retreat for monks and lay visitors alike.

sections.title: A Living Monastery Today
sections.content: Nearly half a century on, Wat Tham Suea remains an active, living monastery — not merely a tourist site. At dawn monks walk for alms and devotees make offerings; on Buddhist holy days it fills with pilgrims. It carries layered meaning as a place of religious practice, nature conservation and local cultural identity.

history.legendText: Folklore tells that as the monk meditated through the dark cave nights, a tiger — far from harming him — lay at the entrance to guard him and ward off evil. When the monk passed away, the tiger's shadow vanished too, leaving only the claw marks on the wall and that tiger-shaped stalactite. To this day, pilgrims who believe the cave's tiger-spirit protects their practice light incense before the tiger stone and the Buddha footprint.

reviews.title: Visitor Reviews
reviews.declaration: The reviews below are compiled visitor feedback to help you understand the real experience. See more on Google Maps.

items.name: Lin Xiaotong
items.text: Reaching the top was so worth it! The golden Buddha glitters in the sun and the Krabi plain stretches endlessly. Bring water and wear trainers.

items.name: David Parker
items.text: 1,237 steps are tiring but the monkeys are cute and the summit view is superb. Go early — fewer people and less heat.

items.name: Suchart Wongthai
items.text: As a devotee I found it solemn and the caves and Buddha impressive. Only note: the steps are slippery, so elders and kids should go slowly.

items.name: Aiko Tanaka
items.text: Free entry was a pleasant surprise and the monks are friendly. Watching sunset from the top was the most unforgettable moment of my Krabi trip.

reviews.moreReviews: See more reviews on Google Maps

faq.title: Before You Visit
faq.subtitle: Common questions about the climb, tickets, dress code and the best time to go — answered in one place.

items.q: How many steps are there to the top?
items.a: The staircase is signed as 1,237 steps to the golden Buddha at the summit; after later renovation some sources now count 1,260. Either way it is steep and partly unshaded — the climb usually takes 30–60 minutes, so pace yourself.
The temple grounds are generally open daily from about 06:00 to 18:00, and the staircase closes at dusk. Come early — you avoid the midday heat and the summit is at its clearest.
Entry to the temple, the summit and the caves is free, with optional donations. Parking or guide services may charge a small fee.

items.q: When is the best time to visit?
items.a: Early morning (after opening) or late afternoon avoids the midday heat and gives the best light and sunsets. In the rainy season watch for slippery steps.
As a Buddhist site, cover shoulders and knees and remove shoes in the main hall. A sarong or long pants are handy to bring.
Macaques are used to people but can be aggressive — do not feed, tease or flash food, and secure glasses and phones.

items.q: How do I get there from Krabi town or Ao Nang?
items.a: From Krabi town the easiest option is a shared blue songthaew, or a taxi / rented motorbike heading north on Route 4034 for about 7 km. From Ao Nang it is noticeably further, so a taxi, Grab or rented scooter is the practical choice — allow extra time and agree the fare before you set off.

weather.title: Weather Forecast & 7-Day Outlook
weather.subtitle: Check the sky before you climb. The 1,237-step staircase is fully exposed, so felt temperature, rain probability and UV intensity decide how comfortable the ascent will be. Below we translate the numbers into what to wear, how to plan and what to pack.

verdict.ok: Great conditions — go ahead with your plan
verdict.info: Fine to head out — check the short notes below
verdict.warn: Go if you like, but leave slack in the plan; the sky may turn
verdict.danger: Not advisable on your original plan — please reshuffle your day

weather.alertNoneNote: Mountain weather shifts quickly, so no warning does not mean no risk. Have one more look at the live figures before you set off.
weather.coastNote: Nearshore figures are regional reference values. Before entering the water, follow the flags and lifeguard advice on the day.

outfit.hot: Hot and sunny — light, breathable short sleeves and trousers. Quick-dry fabric beats cotton by a wide margin.
outfit.warm: Mild and warm — short sleeves plus a thin layer is plenty, and easy to shed once you heat up.
outfit.cool: Chilly at either end of the day. Bring a light jacket you can pull on going up and coming down.
outfit.tempSwing: The day-night gap is noticeable, so pair a light jacket with short sleeves for easy layering.
outfit.wet: You will get rained on. Wear a waterproof shell or quick-dry clothing, and skip absorbent cotton trousers.
outfit.humid: Humid and sticky — choose quick-dry, breathable fabric rather than heavy fitted cotton.
outfit.windy: Fairly windy. Skip flowing long skirts and wide-brim hats; they get blown about badly.
outfit.default: Just wear something light and easy to walk in — comfort and freedom of movement come first.

plan.sunny: Clear and bright — ideal for outdoor sightseeing, and good for sunrise or sunset.
plan.overcast: Soft light, great for photos and no harsh sun — a good day to wander slowly.
plan.drizzle: Light drizzle about. Outdoor experiences lose some shine and the steps turn slick, so slow down.
plan.rainLikely: Rain is likely. Prioritise sheltered stops such as the cave and indoor areas, and push the climb and the coast later.
plan.heavyRain: Heavy rain expected — avoid outdoor plans entirely and steer clear of valleys and low-lying ground.
plan.thunder: Thunderstorms around. Do not climb, do not linger near water or under trees; the summit and exposed steps are the worst places.
plan.hot: Temperatures are high. Squeeze outdoor time into early morning and late afternoon, and stay in shade at midday.
plan.uvHigh: UV is strong. Avoid midday and get your sunscreen on before you leave.
plan.foggy: Poor visibility. Mountain and sea views lose much of their value, and navigation on the climb gets harder.
plan.good: Ordinary conditions — your original plan is fine, just keep an eye on the sky.
plan.window: Aim for {start}–{end}: that is when rain chance is lowest and the temperature is most comfortable.
plan.windowNone: No clear good-weather window in the next 12 hours — check the forecast once more before you head out.

scene.mountainCalm: The exposed summit is windier and cooler than the base — have a jacket ready before you head up.
scene.mountainWind: Summit winds are noticeably stronger. Hold the rail, stow hats and loose items, then take your photos.
scene.mountainStorm: If thunder arrives, descend immediately — never shelter on the steps or the summit platform.
scene.mountainWet: Steps are slippery. On the way down, step sideways and slowly, hold the rail, and spare your knees.
scene.caveCool: The cave stays cool year-round and is well below outdoor temperature — a good place to rest and cool off.
scene.caveWet: The cave floor is damp and water drips from the walls. Watch your footing and keep hands off the rock.
scene.forestRepel: Mosquitoes are active in the forest — apply repellent to exposed skin beforehand.
scene.forestSlick: Forest paths turn soft and slick; deep-tread soles keep you steadier.
scene.waterFlow: Water levels rise quickly after rain — mind the wet stones if you go near the water.
scene.coastWave: Waves are around {h} m, still within a swimmer-friendly range, but check the flags on site.
scene.coastAlert: Waves are around {h} m and the sea is rough — not a day to swim, and keep clear of rocks and the water's edge.
scene.coastTemp: Sea temperature is about {t}°C, milder than the air; after a long soak, watch for chills on leaving the water.
scene.coastTide: The next high tide is around {high} and low tide around {low} — plan shell-hunting and photos around the tide.

thunder.x: Lightning is active. Reshuffle your plan and stay away from the summit, the water and large trees, and do not stop on exposed steps.

heavyRain.x: Significant rainfall is expected. Avoid valleys, low ground and steep slopes, and watch for flash floods, rockfall and flooding on the steps.

wind.x: Winds are strong, felt even more so at height. Keep your footing, secure loose items, and expect hats to blow away.

fog.x: Visibility is poor and the mountain path is hard to read. Postpone the climb.

heat.x: Felt temperature is very high. Avoid long outdoor exposure in the afternoon and drink steadily to prevent heat exhaustion.

heatWatch.x: Felt temperature is high. Try to avoid climbing at midday and carry plenty of water.

cold.x: Temperatures are low — dress for the cold, especially on the windy summit.

weather.unavailable: Live data could not be retrieved right now, which is usually a brief network or data-service interruption. Please refresh the page shortly. In the meantime you can still plan by season using the table below.

facilities.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities (Type-Level Overview)
facilities.subtitle: What follows describes facility types objectively so you can plan ahead. No specific business is recommended or rated.
facilities.neutralNotice: This is a non-profit educational site with no commercial partnership with any business. All facility information is given only as a type-level overview; for actual conditions, please rely on on-site signage.
tips: Facilities cluster near the temple gate and thin out the higher you go — sort out water, toilets and supplies before you start climbing.
The temple is a religious site and its facilities primarily serve worshippers. During peak season or ceremonies, please give way to elders and local devotees.
Prices, opening hours and availability can change at any time, so this page deliberately avoids quoting specific figures.
During the monsoon, water pressure and power can fluctuate briefly; charge devices and fill water bottles while you are still in town.

categories.title: Restrooms (WC)
categories.summary: Public restrooms are concentrated at the temple gate and the main courtyard — the most convenient spot and effectively the last one before the climb.
points: Use them before you start; there are no restrooms along the main staircase or at the summit.
The busiest window is after 09:00 and queues are likely in high season.
Some points do not stock soap or tissue, so carry wet wipes.

categories.title: Parking
categories.summary: Vehicle parking areas sit close to the temple gate, mostly sized for cars and motorbikes.
points: Spaces tighten in high season and during the morning; arriving before 08:00 helps.
Most parking surfaces are unpaved and can hold water in the rainy season.
Do not use bays reserved for monks or service vehicles, and never park in the access lane.

categories.title: Food & Dining
categories.summary: Several types of eateries gather around the temple gate, focused on southern Thai home cooking, noodles, coffee and cold drinks.
points: Types range from sit-down shophouses to roadside carts and drink stalls, with wide variation in price and hygiene.
Eat lightly before climbing — neither on an empty stomach nor overly full.
Alcohol is not permitted within the temple grounds, and eating inside the halls is not appropriate.

categories.title: Accommodation
categories.summary: Accommodation is concentrated in Krabi town and the coastal tourist areas; the temple itself has no guest rooms.
points: Types include town hotels, hostels, resorts and homestays, differing in price band and how easily you reach the trailhead.
If you plan a dawn summit, prioritise a stay within a 10–15 minute drive of the gate.
The temple and its meditation forest do not host overnight visitors — camping is not permitted.

categories.title: Shops & Supplies
categories.summary: Convenience stores, pharmacies and supermarkets are mostly in Krabi town and along the main highway.
points: Stock up in town on drinking water, electrolyte drinks, sunscreen and insect repellent.
Water sold near the gate usually costs more than in town, so compare as you need.
Finish fruit and snacks before you climb — carried food invites macaque snatching.

categories.title: Fuel
categories.summary: Petrol stations sit mainly in Krabi town and along the main road towards the temple.
points: Types include branded stations and smaller independent pumps; opening hours are not uniform.
On a rented motorbike, fill the tank and check tyre pressure and brakes before setting off.
There is no fuel on the hill road, so allow a comfortable margin.

categories.title: EV Charging
categories.summary: Charging points are concentrated in town and at large commercial sites; the temple and gate area effectively have none.
points: Types split between destination slow chargers and rapid chargers, and availability varies sharply by location.
If you drive an EV, charge in town and keep a comfortable round-trip reserve.
Do not run cables from the temple or neighbouring businesses to charge.

categories.title: Medical & Pharmacy
categories.summary: General hospitals and clinics are in Krabi town, while pharmacies are more widely distributed, including along the highway.
points: The common issues are twisted ankles, grazes, heat exhaustion and dehydration — carry a basic first-aid kit.
If you have knee trouble, bring a support and slow down considerably on the descent.
Stop climbing and seek help immediately if you feel chest tightness, dizziness or persistent palpitations.

categories.title: Money & Payment
categories.summary: ATMs and exchange counters cluster in town and the tourist areas; around the temple, cash is the norm.
points: Donation boxes accept cash only, so keep some small banknotes with you.
Small eateries and stalls may not accept electronic payment — ask first.
Withdraw from a proper, sheltered machine rather than using an isolated street-side ATM.

categories.title: Water & Refills
categories.summary: Water is sold and supplied around the gate and main courtyard; there is none along the main staircase or at the top.
points: Carry 1–2 litres for the round trip, and more again in the hot season.
Drinking large volumes of plain water does not replace the electrolytes lost in sweat — pair it with a sodium-containing drink.
Water is scarce on the hill, so avoid long, open-ended rinsing.

categories.title: Connectivity
categories.summary: Mobile coverage is reliable in town and along the main road, but can fade intermittently mid-slope and at the summit.
points: Save maps and your itinerary offline before you leave.
Some areas of the temple ask for quiet or restrict photography — follow on-site notices.
If you climb alone, tell someone your plan and agree a return time.

categories.title: Accessibility & Special Needs
categories.summary: The lower temple areas are comparatively level; the main staircase is traditional stone and has no step-free alternative.
points: The main courtyard and cave temple can be explored on the flat without climbing.
Traditional paving limits wheelchair access, so check conditions on the day in advance.
Older visitors can wait in a rest area or at the viewpoint while companions make the climb.

categories.title: Infants & Children
categories.summary: There are rest areas around the gate, but no dedicated parent-and-baby facilities.
points: For infants, a carrier works far better than a pushchair — the main staircase is not pushchair-friendly.
Prepare formula and hot water in town or at your accommodation; the hill is impractical for it.
Children must be held or guided the whole way — never let them run on the steps.

categories.title: Offerings & Incense
categories.summary: The temple provides incense, flowers and offering items through its own channels, as is standard at a religious site.
points: Make offerings through the temple's designated points, not through hawkers of unknown origin.
Do not express goodwill by releasing non-native species — it damages the local ecology.
Donation boxes take cash only; the amount is up to you and the intention matters more than the sum.

seasons.title: Quarterly Visiting Strategy Table
seasons.subtitle: A combined reading of weather, water and wildlife — drawn from long-term climate normals and public material from official meteorological, marine and ecological authorities.

rows.weather: The most comfortable stretch of the year. The northeast monsoon dominates, rain days are at their fewest, daytime runs 28–32°C with 22–24°C at dawn, humidity is low and visibility is good.
rows.water: Streams and limestone seepage drop, so the staircase is dry and stable overall; nearshore water is clear and the sea relatively calm.
rows.wildlife: Long-tailed macaques forage around the gate and forest edge, birds and butterflies are active through the day, and hornbills or raptors occasionally circle overhead.
rows.advice: The best climbing window of the year. Start between 06:00 and 08:00 to avoid the mid-morning tour groups, and still carry around one litre of water.

rows.weather: Temperatures peak, commonly 33–36°C by day with April the hottest. Afternoon UV index often reaches 10–12, while rainfall stays relatively scarce.
rows.water: Surfaces dry out and the gate water points come under pressure; sea temperatures rise, making afternoon sea conditions more likely to deteriorate.
rows.wildlife: Macaques enter breeding and infant-rearing, with pronounced protective behaviour and more aggression around food; mosquitoes and insects increase.
rows.advice: Start around 06:00 and finish both the ascent and descent before 10:30. Carry 1.5–2 litres plus electrolytes, and avoid midday exposure.

rows.weather: The southwest monsoon brings frequent convective rain, usually short and intense in the afternoon. Rain days rise markedly and humidity stays above 80%.
rows.water: The staircase stays wet, and algae and silt on the stone sharply reduce grip; thunderstorms can create temporary runoff in the valleys.
rows.wildlife: Amphibians and reptiles become more active, frogs and insects appear in numbers after rain, and ferns and fungi flourish in the understorey.
rows.advice: Climb in the morning rain window and wear deep-tread shoes. Descend immediately at the first thunder and do not linger on the exposed summit.

rows.weather: The wettest stretch of the year, with sustained rain and thunderstorms together and occasional tropical depression influence. Winds shift from southwest to northeast.
rows.water: Surface runoff is at its strongest and rock stays slippery for longer; nearshore water turns turbid and underwater visibility drops.
rows.wildlife: Insects and frogs peak for the year, snakes are occasionally recorded, and plants enter their fullest growing phase with the densest canopy.
rows.advice: Work to weather windows and never force a climb on a rain day. Follow official warnings and carry spare clothing and dry bags.

seasons.sourceNote: Basis: long-term climate normals from Thailand's official meteorological authority, public material from the national parks and wildlife conservation authority and the marine and coastal resources authority, cross-checked against historical daily weather records.

legend.title: Weather indicators
legend.text: Built on long-term local climate normals, overlaid with monthly rain-day counts and the frequency of extreme heat.

legend.title: Water & ground
legend.text: Assesses step wetness, runoff intensity and nearshore sea state for their effect on walking safety and the view.

legend.title: Wildlife

plans.title: Visiting Plans Tailored to Different Travellers
plans.subtitle: Three targeted routes: families with children / photography and nature / low-mobility and accessibility. Pick by group make-up and preferred pace.

items.name: Families with children
items.audience: Households travelling with toddlers or school-age children, moving slowly with plenty of breaks.
items.route: Temple gate → parking → restrooms → cave temple and main hall → viewpoint (no summit) → return the same way. If a child has energy left, one adult can continue to the top while the other waits at the viewpoint.
highlights: The cave temple and main hall deliver the most reward for the least effort
The viewpoint looks out over Krabi town and the karst ranges
Macaques, butterflies and limestone vegetation along the way
cautions: Carrying a toddler the whole way to the summit is not advisable — the main steps are narrow and steep
Never feed or tease the macaques, and keep food and plastic bags out of sight
Schedule water and rest every 20–30 minutes
Avoid midday; aim for the early morning instead

items.name: Photography & nature
items.audience: Visitors whose main purpose is landscape, cultural and ecological photography.
items.route: Reach the gate before sunrise → low-angle shots of the temple buildings and morning chanting → ascend slowly for mist and golden light → multiple summit angles on the golden Buddha → descend shooting rock faces and vegetation detail.
highlights: The golden chedi and layered cloud sea in front-lit morning light
Rock texture and clinging vegetation on the karst cliffs
Low cloud wrapping the mid-slope after rain
cautions: Summit space is limited — keep tripods clear of the walking line
Drone use must follow local regulations and temple rules; do not launch without permission
Ask before photographing monks or worshippers
Strong UV and wind-blown dust: protect lenses and sensors

items.name: Low mobility & accessible visits
items.audience: Older visitors, people with knee problems, those recovering from surgery, or anyone needing more accessible circulation.
items.route: Parking → the comparatively level main courtyard → cave temple → rest area or viewpoint → return. The whole route avoids the 1,237-step main staircase.
highlights: The main courtyard has a comparatively even surface for slow walking
The cave temple and main hall sit roughly on one level — no climbing
Sit and rest in the courtyard or viewpoint and listen to wind in the trees
cautions: Traditional paving restricts wheelchair use, so confirm conditions on the day
Surfaces are slippery in the monsoon — go with a companion
Hydrate and seek shade during hot hours
Stop climbing and seek help immediately if you feel chest tightness or dizziness

itinerary.title: Recommended General Visiting Routes
itinerary.subtitle: A half-day essentials version and a full-day in-depth version — take whichever suits your energy and schedule. The one rule is to climb during the coolest hours of the day.

half.title: Half-day route (essentials)
half.note: For visitors with limited time and moderate fitness. The point is to dodge crowds and heat, and to spend your energy on the climb itself.

steps.title: Arrive at the gate
steps.text: Come around sunrise when it is coolest, light is softest and parking is easiest. Use the restroom and check your water supply.

steps.title: Tour the cave temple
steps.text: Start with the lower cave temple and main hall, taking in the morning chanting and offering atmosphere. No climbing required here.

steps.title: Begin the ascent
steps.text: Start up the main staircase. The early section is gentler, the middle is steepest — use short steps and an even breathing rhythm, resting every 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Reach the summit
steps.text: Spend around 30 minutes at the golden Buddha and viewpoint, looking over Krabi town, the mangroves and the distant karst ranges.

steps.title: Descend
steps.text: The descent loads your knees more, so step sideways, hold the rail and slow down further when the stone is wet.

steps.title: Wrap up
steps.text: Back at the gate, eat breakfast and replace water and electrolytes, closing out the half-day route.

full.title: Full-day route (in-depth)
full.note: Beyond the summit, this adds the temple fringes, nearby nature and a midday retreat from the heat — for visitors with time who want a complete understanding of the site.

steps.title: Gate and morning offerings
steps.text: Watch devotees make morning offerings and monks on alms round — the most direct window into the daily life of a southern Thai temple.

steps.title: Detailed cave temple visit
steps.text: Study the stalactites, the reclining Buddha and the displays about the tiger-paw-like rock marks, and note the natural patterning on the walls.

steps.title: Ascend
steps.text: Climb at the half-day pace, reserving the coolest hours for the most strenuous section.

steps.title: Time on the summit
steps.text: Allow 40–60 minutes to photograph, sit quietly, and observe macaque social behaviour and the stunted summit vegetation.

steps.title: Descend and breakfast
steps.text: After coming down, eat around the temple with a focus on electrolytes and carbohydrates.

steps.title: Temple fringes and forest paths
steps.text: Walk slowly along the forest paths, observing the vertical layering of limestone forest and the movement of butterflies and birds.

steps.title: Midday shelter
steps.text: Stay in the shade or return to town during peak heat — avoid prolonged exposure on the unshaded steps.

steps.title: Return at dusk or explore onward
steps.text: In the cool and monsoon seasons you can return uphill for sunset, or head to the nearby coast to link the water system and karst landforms into one continuous geographic story.

tip.title: Pacing note
tip.text: Half day or full day, the principle is the same: climb during the coolest, best-lit hours. The staircase itself is not hard — climbing it under a 33°C sun is.

responsible.title: Reading the Landscape, and Visiting Responsibly
responsible.subtitle: Treat this hill as a textbook of geology and ecology — and visit without adding to its burden.

science.title: How the karst formed
science.text: The limestone massif the temple sits on formed in the ancient Tethys Sea around 250 million years ago. Coral and shell deposits built thick limestone beds, which plate uplift and long tropical rainfall dissolution then carved into the steep isolated peaks, caves and stalactites seen today. Tham is the Thai word for cave.

science.title: Vertical layering in limestone forest
science.text: Tropical limestone forest has extremely thin, fast-draining soil, so plants evolved strategies such as rooting onto bare rock and storing water in their leaves. Ferns and climbers tolerant of shade occupy the base, drought-tolerant scrub the mid-slope, and stunted trees with epiphytes the summit — a clear vertical sequence.

science.title: Living alongside macaques
science.text: The long-tailed macaques near the gate are highly adapted to people, but feeding them changes their foraging behaviour and raises the risk of snatching and bites. Keep at least three metres away, avoid challenging eye contact, never carry exposed food, and do not let children approach alone.

science.title: The tiger-cave legend and how the temple grew
science.text: The name comes from natural markings on the rock wall resembling a tiger's paw, which hunters and villagers took as evidence that tigers once lived here. In the late 20th century forest monks settled and built huts, gradually shaping today's site — a combination of cave, meditation forest and hilltop chedi.

science.title: Temple etiquette in Theravada practice
science.text: Remove shoes before entering halls and dress so shoulders and knees are covered; do not climb on or touch Buddha images. Avoid physical contact with monks — women especially — and offer items with the right hand. Keep quiet in meditation and chanting areas and silence your phone.

duties.title: Look, don't touch
duties.text: Stalactites and stalagmites grow over tens of thousands of years, and oils and sweat from a single touch can end that growth. Do not touch, climb on or carve into them.

duties.title: Carry your waste back down
duties.text: Bins in the temple and forest are limited, so bring a bag. Fruit peel and food scraps also alter wildlife diets, which makes them waste you need to carry out too.

duties.title: Offer rather than feed
duties.text: If you wish to show respect, use the incense, flowers or vegetarian offerings the temple provides, instead of feeding wildlife or releasing non-native species.

duties.title: Conserve water and power
duties.text: Water and electricity are constrained in the hills. Shorten your water use, switch off what you are not using, and reduce single-use packaging.

duties.title: Respect closures and boundaries
duties.text: Do not enter monks' meditation forest, private areas or closed paths. When you see a no-entry sign, turn back — reconnaissance is not a reason to continue.

duties.title: Respect people and ceremonies
duties.text: Ask before photographing monks, worshippers or an ongoing ceremony. Do not use direct flash, and do not disturb ceremonies with a drone.

duties.title: Never trade safety for a photo
duties.text: Do not shoot from the edge of steep steps, beyond railings or on wet rock. No photograph is worth trading your safety for.

duties.title: Report accurately
duties.text: If you find incorrect information, damaged facilities or environmental damage, tell us or report it directly to the temple and the relevant authorities.

responsible.pledge: This is a non-profit educational site. We do not sell tickets, do not book services on anyone's behalf, and take no commission from any business. All content is compiled from public sources and on-the-ground knowledge, with the aim of helping visitors understand this temple and its surrounding karst ecology safely, respectfully and meaningfully. If you spot a factual error, we welcome the correction.
